title: When You Strongly Disagree, Show Your Work
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that when a leader strongly disagrees with a favored proposal, the way they explain their reasoning matters as much as the conclusion itself. Drawing an analogy to a mathematician showing their calculations, it recommends walking through the facts, options considered, and reasoning steps that led to the opposing view. This transparency doesn't guarantee agreement, but it earns credibility and reduces the instinct in others to dig in defensively. The piece closes by framing 'showing your work' as a demonstration of both thinking and character.
points: How a leader reaches a disagreement matters as much as the conclusion itself.
Walking through the facts, data, and reasoning steps builds credibility even among people who disagree.
There is never a perception of haste when a leader shows their full reasoning process.
Transparency reduces the likelihood that opposing team members will dig in and resist.
'Showing your work' demonstrates both how a leader thinks and who they are as a colleague.
quotes: Those who are suspicious about how you reached the outcome or whether you might have taken a shortcut are reassured when they can examine the steps you used to get there.

Just as we are made more comfortable in the end product produced by a mathematician who shows their calculations, an artist who shares their preliminary drawings, or a mechanic who produces a faulty part before replacing it, we appreciate it when those who disagree show us precisely why.
In the eyes of those who have their views negated, how a leader reaches an alternate conclusion can be as important as the conclusion itself.
By showing their work, leaders and team members are afforded a credibility and positive intent that reduces the friction inherent when negating an opposing view.
In the act of showing their work, leaders demonstrate not only how they think but also who they are as colleagues.
